stories.headline: 'India's tolerance should not be mistaken for weakness': NSA Ajit Doval
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: "Thanks to our intelligence agencies... they did a brilliant job and within a short period of time, we were able to identify the perpetrators and act with precision," 
Ajit Doval
 said. The national security adviser, widely seen as one of the architects of the retaliation for the Pahalgam attack, indicated that India had made up its mind to go to any extent.
"Once it starts, we are willing to go as far as necessary for a nation to preserve its sovereignty and...there are no limits on that. We fight till the last drop of blood. India's being more tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness," Doval said, confirming that the terrorists who had targeted their victims on the basis of faith had breached the country's pain threshold.

The perpetrators had audaciously taunted the Indian leadership, daring it to retaliate. "They (Pahalgam terrorists) had told victims that 'jaake Modi ko bol do jo kar sakta hai kar le'," the NSA recalled.
Doval said India had decided at the outset that the operation would focus on destroying enemy camps associated with the Pahalgam attack, which took place on April 22, 2025, claiming the lives of 26 innocent people.
"We wanted the Pakistan Army to realise that this support to terrorism or inability to take effective action against the terrorists is something which is not tolerable to us... Basically, the world is very clear: India's generosity or India's being more tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness," he said.
The NSA described 
Operation Sindoor
 as evidence of India's growing technological and military capabilities.

briefs.headline: With no centres to hear, panic buttons in buses lie idle
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: A parliamentary panel has taken note of a curious case involving emergency alert buttons in buses. While the switches cost just Rs 15-20 each, they have largely remained unused because there are no dedicated centres to respond to alerts. Bus operators told the panel they are still required to pay Rs 2,500 to Rs 25,000 per vehicle to have the switches tested during mandatory fitness tests.
The latest report of the parliamentary standing committee on transport, tourism and culture, headed by JDU's Sanjay Jha, noted that the buttons were made mandatory after the 2012 Nirbhaya case as a safety measure for women passengers.
The report said the road transport ministry informed the panel that in several states, the system had been connected to emergency response number 112. It also said there were many instances of false alarms, prompting some states to "disengage" them.
"The ministry wishes the system restored, while am-ong operators there is a feeling that it should be dispensed with," the report said. A committee member observed if the system was not effective, it was not fair to charge so much for it. One member asked why CCTV could not be installed. The ministry said cameras were being made mandatory in new buses.
Share your thoughts in the comments
Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
The committee recommended that the programme to install emergency buttons, call facilities and vehicle location tracking devices in public transport vehicles be pursued with states beyond the 16 that have made progress in implementing it.

stories.headline: Back to politics? Karnataka’s campuses set to hear students’ voices again
stories.deck: Cabinet expected to clear proposal at next meeting; rollout likely this academic year
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: As the country was swept up in the CJP’s protests recently, Bengaluru remained largely subdued. While Freedom Park —the city’s only designated venue for protests — witnessed spirited demonstrations, they lacked the scale and intensity seen in New Delhi, Patna and other cities.
The silence on 
Karnataka
’s campuses has deeper roots. It dates back 37 years, when the state govt banned campus politics in higher educational institutions. In 1989, the then Congress govt, led by chief minister Veerendra Patil, ended campus politics amid concerns over violence, political interference and disruption to academics. Though intended as a temporary measure, the ban continued for three-and-a-half decades. Elected student unions were replaced by nominated or advisory councils with little power, often existing largely in name.
But prior to the ban, Karnataka’s higher educational institutions had vibrant campus cultures. Even before electronic voting machines (EVMs) were used in assembly elections, the technology was piloted in student elections at MES College in Bengaluru.
Campuses at Mysore University, Karnatak University in Dharwad and Bangalore University once thrived on political and social discourse. 
Students debated land reforms, linguistic identity, social justice and reservation, while unions represented students before administrations and took up issues such as hostels, scholarships, transport, exams and the concerns of marginalised students. But by the late 1970s and early 1980s, things changed. Political groups gained ground on campuses, and university elections increasingly mirrored rivalries outside. Candidates received backing and funding from political parties, while outsiders and anti-social elements entered campuses. Many candidates were also barely engaged with academics.
At the same time, ideological and caste divisions deepened, triggering clashes and violence. Police became regular fixtures on campuses, academic calendars were disrupted, and managements struggled to maintain order and discipline. It was against this backdrop that the govt decided to put an end to campus elections.
But now, the 
Congress government
, which itself faces a dearth of youth leaders, decided to reintroduce campus elections. In Dec 27, 
DK Shivakumar
, deputy chief minister at the time, formed an 11-member high-power committee under the chairmanship of medical education minister
 Sharan Prakash Patil, asking them to submit a report on the same.
The
 committee has recommended reintroducing student elections. “Student elections are important because they nurture leadership and give natural leaders a pathway into public life. Democracy must also be ingrained early. When students elect their representatives, they learn to stand up for their rights and interests. Otherwise, politics risks becoming the preserve of political families and the wealthy. Leadership should not be limited to those born into privilege,” said Patil.
“However, we will not allow political interference. Students must contest elections independently, without the backing of any political party. Candidates must also be regular students of the college,” he added.
The proposal is expected to be cleared by the cabinet at its next meeting and rolled out in the current academic year.
Ashwathnarayan CN, BJP MLA and for higher education minister, said while initiating student elections is welcome, it should not allow politicisation and remain neutral.
Political observer Sandeep Shastri said student politics is welcome as long as it does not compromise academic quality. However, he rejected any link between the subdued response to the CJP protests in Bengaluru and the absence of campus politics.
“I wouldn’t subscribe to the argument that the CJP movement lacked traction in the state because we don’t have campus politics. They are two different issues. Protests by the younger generation in Bengaluru are generally low-key. The movement gained traction mainly in states where the party in power at the Centre was also in power in the state,” he said.
QUotes
Abhinandan Mirji, Mahanagara Secretary, Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, Bengaluru
Elected student bodies will strengthen student representation and help nurture future leaders. But political parties should not use campus elections to push their ideologies or bring political leaders onto campuses. There must be safeguards for fair elections, including a cap on campaign spending. The election process should also be time-bound so that regular classes are not disrupted
Khalif Belthangady, political strategist
The impact of the absence of student leaders is evident in the state’s political leadership. Karnataka’s current and several former chief ministers have roots in campus politics. With student unions absent for decades, we are increasingly seeing nepotism in politics. Where will new political leaders emerge from if there are no student elections?
Aratrika Dey, All India Students’ Association
AISA is active in several colleges across Bengaluru and Karnataka, but we are not allowed to organise protests on university campuses. Students from marginalised communities continue to face discrimination. Elected student unions are needed to address these issues, not just in govt but also private colleges. Currently, student councils are largely chosen on faculty recommendations, making them less able to raise students’ concerns

stories.headline: Only 354 of Karnataka’s 80,000 engineering students opt for internships in 7th semester
stories.deck: VTU’s Flexibility Programme Receives Cold Response
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Only 354 engineering students have chosen to do an internship in the seventh semester instead of the eighth, in a cold response to 
Visvesvaraya Technological University
 (
VTU
)’s swapping system.
VTU had launched the semester swapping system, permitting its students to pursue an internship in the seventh semester. The usual practice is to complete a project in the seventh semester and an internship in the eighth.
The swapping system aims to ensure that students do not find it hard to land an internship as around 80,000 candidates apply at the same time. It may be recalled that last year, several students ended up with paid internships amid tight competition and confusion.
This year, VTU set the ball rolling for students to choose to pursue an internship in the seventh or eighth semester. “The hope was that half of the students will choose in the seventh semester. With this, things will be smoother in both the semesters. But, only very few students took it up in the seventh semester,” said a VTU official.
VTU is studying the reasons for this refusal to change. “Many students, who are hostelites, find it convenient to complete all the classes by seventh semester and then vacate the hostels. For instance, many of them would be pursuing internships in Bengaluru. 
So, they can vacate the hostel and shift to Bengaluru, thus saving six months of hostel fees,” he said.
“Yet another group of students who wouldn’t want to change are those with supplementary papers. If they complete all the classes in the seventh semester, they will still have time to finish the failed papers in the final semester. If their classes finish only in the eighth semester, they will be worried clearing failed papers will take further time,” he added.
“It will take time to change the mindset of these youngsters. We have to create awareness among principals and students about the advantages of the swapping semester system. We can only advise them; it cannot be made mandatory,” he observed.
A college principal said that students continue to prefer the eighth semester. “Most colleges complete the project work in seventh. Students want to complete all the academic work and have a free mind for eighth so that they can relax. So even though VTU has given the flexibility, it has not been popular. Nobody from my college has opted for it,” he said.

stories.headline: SIR: Karnataka races to issue PRCs, but no clarity on whether document will pass muster
stories.deck: Acknowledging that many voters do not have even one of the 11 documents in the ECI list, the State government had launched a drive to deliver PRCs as well as caste certificates at the doorstep
stories.bodyText:
With the enumeration phase of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) set to end on Monday (August 17), the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) is yet to indicate whether the Permanent Residential Certificate (PRC) that the Election Commission of India itself lists as an indicative document will actually be accepted in the State.
Clarity on this issue is particularly important for voters who would be flagged for logical discrepancies in their enumeration forms and the over 28 lakh unmapped voters who could not find their or their families’ details in the 2002 base roll. Following the release of the draft electoral roll, these voters will be asked to submit one of the 11 documents.
Acknowledging that many voters do not even have one of the 11 documents as per ECI list, the State government had launched a drive to deliver PRCs as well as caste certificates at their doorstep. Yet, as the enumeration deadline approaches, the election machinery has still not made clear whether those certificates will pass muster.
Karnataka CEO V. Anbu Kumar said that he would provide clarity over PRCs “later”. When pointed out that PRC is one of the valid documents mentioned in the ECI’s list of accepted “indicative” documents, the CEO said he “cannot comment on individual document case”.
The CEO’s response
Conditional acceptance
It is to be noted that during the SIR in West Bengal, the ECI, after political intervention, finally agreed to accept PRCs that strictly conformed to specific State government orders — the 1999 framework — and underwent independent verification by Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), instead of treating all PRCs alike.
Similar to how the Karnataka government directed officials to issue PRCs, the Telangana government had also ordered officials to issue Family Register Certificates (FRCs). Recently, however, the Telangana CEO rejected those documents. The FRC is different from the Family Member Certificate (FMC) issued by the State, said the ECI, because it was based on information that had been digitally extracted from ration card data.
The Telangana government order issued on July 25, in the midst of the SIR process there, said it had been decided to launch the FRC with a view of facilitating the delivery of services, ensuring uniformity in the verification of family particulars, and providing a readily accessible record.
While the Telangana government has said it will represent to the EC to reconsider its rejection of FRCs, pointing out that it could deprive a large section of people of their voting rights and put their names at risk of deletion from the SIR, the Congress government in Karnataka has so far been silent on the issue.
Speaking to The Hindu, Booth Level Agents (BLAs) as well as senior Congress members involved in the vigilance teams maintained that they would ensure every eligible person gets a PRC, leaving no clarity over what happens if the Election Commission ultimately decides to subject those very certificates to conditions and verification, as it did in West Bengal.

stories.headline: Security guard held for alleged terror plot targeting Pakistan Army, TTP links in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
The Hebbagodi police have arrested a 23-year-old security guard from West Bengal for allegedly planning to undergo terrorist training and target the Pakistan Army. He allegedly established contact with a suspected member of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) in Afghanistan, according to the FIR.
The accused, identified as Asaful Mallick, is a native of North 24 Parganas district in West Bengal. He had been working as a security guard at a company in Jigani Industrial Area since December 2025. He was staying near APC Circle in Jigani.
The FIR was registered based on a complaint by sub-inspector Srikanth Naykar, who reportedly received information about the accused from an informant.
According to the FIR, the police received information that Mallick was planning to undergo training for a terrorist act against the Pakistan Army. Subsequently, the police gathered information about the suspect and traced him to an under construction building near Jigani. The police detained Mallick and brought him to the station for questioning, the FIR stated.
During questioning, he allegedly told the police that he was angry with the Pakistan Army over alleged atrocities against mosques and people in Pakistan. He allegedly expressed anger over Pakistan’s stance over the Israel-Palestine conflict, according to the FIR.
The police claimed that he had befriended an Afghan national, identified as Imran Haider, through social media channels, whom the FIR describes as a member of the TTP.
According to the police, Mallick allegedly sought Haider’s assistance to join the TTP and travel to Afghanistan. He had allegedly applied for a visa to travel to Afghanistan, but later changed his mind due to financial difficulties and concerns about taking care of his family members, the FIR stated.
The police examined Mallick’s mobile phone and allegedly found chats with Haider on social media, besides several voice calls and audio recordings, according to the FIR.
The police have registered an FIR under Section 113(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Sir M Visvesvaraya Central College and Cubbon Park Metro stations were closed around 7pm as crowds swelled near the event venue, with trains instructed to skip both stations. BMRCL had also announced that Dr BR Ambedkar Vidhana Soudha Metro station would remain closed from 10.30am to 9.30pm Saturday

“Considering the heavy crowding, the operations wing took a decision to temporarily shut the stations during the evening. Trains skipped all three stations, while MG Road and Nadaprabhu Kempegowda stations continued to operate as usual,” a BMRCL official said.
The closures caused difficulties for commuters travelling to and from Vidhana Soudha. MG Road station also witnessed heavy footfall, making access to platforms difficult, as cultural programmes and public activities continued through the evening.

briefs.headline: Independence Day 2026: When Bengaluru’s Vidhana Soudha turned into people’s plaza
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 For a day, the steady stream of vehicles that usually passes through Vidhana Soudha gave way to something far rarer — people. And thousands of them. Families, children, students, office-goers, senior citizens and visitors from different corners of the city took over the grand boulevard outside 
Karnataka
’s seat of power, transforming it into a vibrant public square filled with laughter, music, colour and conversations.
At Freedom Habba, Bengaluru did not merely celebrate Independence Day; it celebrated itself. From toddlers to curious children tugging their parents towards activity zones, the venue buzzed with energy from morning till evening.
While children explored Makkala Habba, many others queued up to experience Freedom Walk, a journey through stories of Karnataka’s contribution to the freedom movement. The Constitution Wall drew crowds eager to trace the evolution of the nation’s founding document.
Elsewhere, the mood was unhurried. Some sat on the lawns soaking in the beauty of Vidhana Soudha; a few sketched the imposing structure and Mahatma Gandhi’s statue, while countless others posed for photographs against the iconic backdrop.
One of the biggest attractions was the cultural parade and performances staged on the road in front of Vidhana Soudha. The stretch that normally echoes with honking traffic came alive with drums, folk music and dancers representing diverse traditions from across Karnataka and India.
Makkala Habba turned learning into play, with kids trying their hand at painting, clay work, flower-making and other DIY activities. A session on waste segregation got them thinking about the four different types of bins and what goes where.
Another attraction was the wish wall, where visitors could write what they wanted India to look like in 2047. Among the messages were wishes for a corruption-free country and a better future.
Beyond the performances and attractions, the habba brought together Kannadigas and non-Kannadigas, long-time Bengalureans and newcomers, creating a shared space to celebrate freedom and belonging. As dusk settled over the illuminated dome and the crowds slowly dispersed, Freedom Habba left behind more than photographs and performances. It offered a glimpse of what public spaces can become when they are handed back to the people — open, welcoming and shared.
‘LET US STAY UNITED’
Aug 15 must become everyone’s first festival. That’s the main intention of Freedom Habba, and that’s why we chose Vidhana Soudha as the venue. Bengaluru is a beautiful city where people from every culture, community and part of India come together. One nation, many cultures, but one city — Namma Bengaluru. Freedom Habba sends a message that after the British, nobody should be allowed to divide us again on any grounds. We are also planning a 10-day festival called Bengaluru Jatare in Dec: 
Krishna Byre Gowda, Bengaluru development minister.VISITORS SPEAKRoopa M & Reeyansh N | from Rajajinagar
I came here with family and my son had a great time at Makkala Habba, where multiple art and craft activities were planned. There are also several activities related to Independence struggle, including Karnataka’s role and its history. This is our first time here, and it’s really good. Usually, we only see 
Independence Day
 celebrated with flag hoisting, but this is a different experience
Anitha Sampath | engineer, Jayanagar
I usually love art and sketching. I have passed by the road near Vidhana Soudha many times, but never stepped inside. We never know when we'll get another opportunity like this. I was very happy to see a drawing activity had been planned. So I thought I shouldn’t miss this opportunity to sketch the building, and I truly loved it
Srimathi Nayak, Vikram Nayak & Antara Nayak | from Hennur
I’ve been living in the city for the past 24 years but have never been inside Vidhana Soudha. I was excited and curious to see what the assembly halls, speaker’s room and other rooms looked like. It’s good govt took this initiative. And since it’s Independence Day, we decided to dress up in the tricolour
Nagraj Nayak | lecturer
I visited the Uttara Kannada stall and it brought back memories of my hometown. Watching artists portray freedom fighters from different districts of Karnataka gave me goosebumps. It felt like we were living through the freedom movement. Such demonstrations are much needed, especially for youngsters
Harikesh Deshmukh | from Belagavi
Freedom Walk took me from the present to those days of the freedom struggle. Kittur Chennamma and Sangolli Rayanna are two great freedom fighters from my hometown, and watching their life stories being portrayed was indeed mesmerising

briefs.headline: 72k jobs, AI varsity, green Bengaluru: CM makes big promises in Independence Day speech
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Jobs for youngsters, artificial intelligence (AI), public safety, and a major infrastructure and environmental push for Bengaluru formed the centrepiece of 
DK Shivakumar
’s maiden Independence Day address as chief minister Saturday, as he unveiled a series of initiatives aimed at preparing 
Karnataka
’s young population for the next phase of economic growth while strengthening Bengaluru as the state’s economic and technology capital.
Hoisting the Tricolour at Field Marshal Manekshaw Parade Ground during the state-level celebrations marking India’s 80th Independence Day, Shivakumar put youth aspirations at the centre of his address, announcing programmes to equip youngsters with skills suited to evolving industry requirements.
Stating that “Yuva Karnataka, Nava Bharat” would be his guiding motto, Shivakumar said investing in youngsters was essential to building a stronger Karnataka. “Neither I nor my govt is satisfied with what has already been achieved. The focus would now be on shaping the present to prepare Karnataka for the future,” he said.
CM’s Jobs Mission
Seeking to expand employment opportunities across sectors, Shivakumar announced the CM’s Jobs Mission, reiterating govt’s commitment to filling vacant posts. “The recruitment process for 72,000 key vacancies across departments has commenced, with notifications for all the posts expected within the next six months,” he said.
Govt will also launch Yuva Udyoga Setu, a digital platform connecting job seekers, employers and educational institutions. Around 100 govt ITIs will be transformed into employment-oriented campuses in partnership with industries, with an initial target of creating employment opportunities for 10,000 youngsters. Under Udyoga Nidhi, entrepreneurs creating jobs in the state’s 10 most backward districts will receive an incentive of Rs 2,500 per new job every month for two years. The scheme aims to generate one lakh jobs.
Coding & AI university
AI will form another major pillar of govt’s growth strategy. Shivakumar announced plans for a govt-driven AI university in Bengaluru, aimed at strengthening AI education, research, innovation, and industry collaboration. He said AI certificate courses would begin at the university by Jan 2027, while the state would develop a wider AI ecosystem to equip its workforce with skills needed for emerging technologies.
Acknowledging that the emerging era belonged to youngsters, Shivakumar said govt was designing initiatives to help them compete globally. “We’re designing a wide range of initiatives to prepare today’s youth to compete successfully on the global stage and shape a new future for themselves,” he said, adding that govt will soon launch ‘AI Akshara Abhiyana’ and ‘Coding Gurukul’, with free special classes to provide students with an opportunity to learn AI and coding skills.
Putting safety first
Alongside the youth and technology agenda, Shivakumar announced a major overhaul of policing in Bengaluru. The city police commissionerate will be reorganised into five commissionerates, with new police stations to be established wherever necessary.
The move, Shivakumar said, would strengthen law and order and bring policing closer to Bengaluru’s rapidly expanding neighbourhoods. A dedicated anti-rowdy squad will also be constituted to crack down on anti-social elements and create a fear-free environment for citizens.
Sustainable makeover
To tackle pollution and environmental pressures arising from traffic and rapid urbanisation, govt will develop five tree parks modelled on Lalbagh, the CM promised.
The state also plans to rejuvenate seven lakes to improve groundwater recharge and strengthen Bengaluru’s drinking water security. The waterbodies identified are Hesaraghatta, Bettada Kote, Hoskote, Ele Mallappa Shetty, Bannerghatta, Bagalur, and Byramangala.
These announcements come alongside govt’s larger Bengaluru development agenda, with Rs 1.5 lakh crore worth of infrastructure projects that have already been taken up across the city, including Phase III of Namma Metro and the long-pending Peripheral Ring Road project, now revived as the 117km Bengaluru Business Corridor.
For farmers whose land is acquired for the project, govt has announced a compensation package comprising cash compensation, TDR, developed residential and commercial sites, and Floor Area Ratio benefits.

briefs.headline: Parking rates may double on Bengaluru’s busiest commercial stretches under draft rules
briefs.deck: The draft rules, published on August 11, mandate city corporations to categorise all stretches into three types; type A, defined as a commercial road that attracts people from across the city, will have a higher charge structure
briefs.bodyText:
If the Karnataka government notifies the draft Greater Bengaluru Authority (Parking) Rules, 2026, the fee for parking in commercial hubs such as M.G. Road and Brigade Road will likely increase by more than twofold from the current charges.
The draft rules, published on August 11, mandate city corporations to categorise all stretches into three types. Type A, defined as a commercial road that attracts people from across the city, will have a higher charge structure.
There are several such stretches in Bengaluru, including Kalyan Nagar Main Road, Sampige Road, Lavelle Road, Koramangala Main Road, and Indiranagar’s 80 Feet and 100 Feet roads, among others.
According to the suggested parking fee structure, two-wheelers and cars along such stretches will be charged ₹40 per hour. For off-street parking, two-wheelers will have to pay ₹20 per hour, while four-wheelers will have to pay ₹40 per hour.
In contrast, the current parking fee on several stretches that qualify as Category A is nominal, at ₹15 per hour for two-wheelers and ₹30 for cars. even for off-street parking, the fee will see a 33.3% increase.
The increase will be a financial burden for several office-goers, especially those who have offices in Central Bengaluru. Due to a lack of space and the dominance of commercial establishments, several offices do not have parking spaces, forcing employees to use on-street parking.
Navya R., a resident of north Bengaluru who commutes to central Bengaluru, says that without the mass expansion of public transport, bringing in such a system will be a huge financial burden.
“To create off-street parking, there is a severe dearth of land in central Bengaluru. So, what will commuters do?” she questioned.
A source who was part of the consultant departments for the policy explained that the rationale behind hiking the price is to minimise on-street parking to a greater extent on arterial and sub-arterial roads. “If parking can be limited on such major roads, the result will have a positive impact on commute times. When off-street parking expands and the demand for on-street parking shifts towards the former, it will have a greater impact,” the official opined.

briefs.headline: Couple found dead at their house in Bengaluru’s Rajagopalnagar
briefs.bodyText:
A 32-year-old man and his wife were found dead at their house under suspicious circumstances in northwest Bengaluru’s Rajagopalnagar on Friday, police said.
The deceased have been identified as Sumanth Jain, a native of Dakshina Kannada, and his 28-year-old wife, Padmavathi. The couple had been married for over three years and had been residing in a rented house near Hegganahalli for the past four months.
According to the police, the couple allegedly had a fight over a marital issue on Thursday night, which escalated and might have ended with Jain killing his wife and subsequently reportedly taking his own life out of fear of the consequences.
The incident came to light when Jain’s relatives arrived at his house. An investigator in the case told The Hindu that Jain had sent a voice message to his mother on Friday at 1.30 a.m., saying that he was taking his life and that she could take his belongings. However, the mother checked the phone later in the day and tried to call him multiple times.
“All calls to him went unanswered, prompting Jain’s mother to call a relative to check on her son. When they went to his house on Friday evening, the incident came to light and we were informed subsequently,” the officer said.
The officer noted that the police are yet to establish how he allegedly killed his wife and what the trigger point was. Police have sent both bodies for post-mortem, and the exact cause of death will only be known after the report is received. They have also not ruled out the possibility of self-harm by both.
For now, Rajagopalnagar police have registered an FIR under Section 103 of the BNS, which deals with murder. In addition, an Unnatural Death Report (UDR) has also been filed.
According to the police, Jain worked as a civil engineer at a company in Nandini Layout, while Padmavathi also worked as an engineer at a company in east Bengaluru’s Whitefield. The bodies of the deceased will be handed over to their families after the post-mortem.

briefs.deck: Following Medha Prithviraj’s death, residents have been demanding better roads in Electronics City Phase 1. While most roads in the area are narrow and pothole-filled, several other stretches have been dug up for civic works.
briefs.bodyText:
The protest that erupted after a 32-year-old woman died in a road accident in Electronics City Phase 2 is an outcome of years of anger against the municipal administration, as local residents have consistently been protesting over poor road infrastructure in the area.
About 400 people participated in a candlelight protest against the administration after Medha Prithviraj, a resident of the area, was run over by a small goods vehicle on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).
According to the police, Medha was pillion-riding on a two-wheeler with her friend on their way to the office when the incident unfolded near the Venkateshwara Temple arch in Ananth Nagar. The driver reportedly applied the brakes to avoid a crash as the vehicle in front also applied sudden brakes. The two-wheeler allegedly skidded, causing both to fall. The rider narrowly escaped, but a goods vehicle coming from the opposite direction ran over Medha, killing her on the spot.
As officers from the municipal administration, Bengaluru city police, and traffic police gathered near the temple arch, residents poured in with questions and demanded accountability. This resulted in a chaotic exchange, prompting the officials to leave the place.
‘Braking caused accident’
Later, the municipal administration claimed that the accident was not an outcome of a bad road but was instead caused by the application of immediate brakes, stressing that the stretch had been recently asphalted.
A source in the traffic police told The Hindu that CUT FOR PRINT even the complainant in the case, the person who was driving the two-wheeler, had also said that he had applied the brakes to avoid a crash.
The officer, however, admitted that the accident was a flashpoint, as the protesters were actually demanding better roads. TILL HERE several stretches are dug up around the locality for civic works, and most roads in the area are narrow.
OPTIONAL FOR PRINT The Hindu, in December, had reported on the infrastructure collapse in the exact locality and surrounding areas. TILL HERE
Poor infrastruture
The area suffers from poorly developed facilities. The connecting roads are either muddy or filled with large craters, and garbage lies strewn around. While a few roads have been taken up for works, the area still suffers from poor infrastructure.
Despite many issues, the suburb is expanding rapidly as rents are relatively lower here than in other parts of the interior city. Many residents in the area have offices in east, south, or central Bengaluru.
The Yellow Line Metro has provided much-needed transport infrastructure for the area, as the Huskur, Hebbagodi, and Bommansandra Metro stations are closer to the locality. In addition, the Heelalige railway station, where six trains halt daily, is also nearby. While office-goers utilise the public transport, accessing it is not easy.
Residents demand better roads
“All these roads are not only narrow, but also the administration has either taken up works on these stretches in the monsoon season or the roads are riddled with large craters. So, commuting during peak hours is a Herculean task every day,” said a resident.
Sowmya Shankar, another resident of Glass Factory Layout, explained that people have to use their own vehicles to reach Metro stations, as there are very limited bus options. “Even autorickshaws don’t come to this area because of bad infrastructure, and if they are stuck in traffic, getting out is a task,” she said.
She further alleged that despite residents’ sustained demands, there has been no improvement in the infrastructure at all.

briefs.headline: Proposed parking charges a solution or a price on Bengaluru’s traffic problem?
briefs.bodyText:
Will the proposed draft parking policy actually ease congestion or just put a price on a problem the city has failed to address for years?
While transport experts argue that parking charges must “discourage” owners from parking their vehicles in congested areas, others argue that levying parking charges without fixing public infrastructure makes citizens pay for a problem that governments helped create.
Demand management
For professor and convenor of the IISc Sustainable Transportation Lab (IST Lab) Ashish Verma, the biggest mistake would be to approach the policy as a way of meeting the city’s demand for parking. The objective should be to reduce the demand for private vehicles in places that are already congested, he said.
“The idea should not be to assess the demand for parking in different areas and accordingly provide adequate supply for parking,” he said. The solution is to make parking restrictive in the city’s most congested areas- both by reducing available spaces and making parking more expensive, particularly during peak periods, he said, arguing that parking should be used “as a demand management measure”.
While restricting cars immediately raises the question of what happens to the people who currently depend on them, that alternative, Prof. Verma said, has to be built alongside the parking policy rather than after it.
Disincentivise multiple car buyers
Dattaraya Devare, an environmental activist who has been championing paid parking, believes the price itself can influence vehicle ownership and use.
“Residential parking could be pricier, but it can be managed by introducing fee slabs based on the particular period when the car was bought. The move will disincentivise people from owning multiple cars,” he said.
Alternatives
But that argument assumes residents have enough choice to respond to the price. Srikanth Narasimhan, founder and general secretary of the Bengaluru Navanirmana Party (BNP), argues that this is what Bengaluru lacks.
Mr. Narasimhan opposed the proposed parking charges based on the premise that the government needs to first provide citizens with real alternatives and take responsibility for the parking crisis.
“While parking charges are not inherently wrong, charging citizens for parking without alternatives is unfair. What choice does a citizen have when public transport is still inadequate?” he questioned, pointing out to the delayed suburban rail, the limited growth of the BMTC fleet, weak last-mile connectivity, delays in metro projects and poor footpaths.
Lack of space
There is also a question of how the existing residential parking system can be regulated at all.
N.S. Mukunda, founder-member of Bengaluru Praja Vedike, said residents may actually be willing to pay for permits if doing so guarantees them a designated space and eliminates the daily disputes over who can park on a particular stretch of road.
“Many disputes arise over parking spaces on streets, so if the authorities allot designated parking spaces on the road, those who want to avoid such hassles will easily obtain a permit,” he said.
But that immediately creates another problem- where will these spaces come from? Bengaluru has very little vacant land available for large-scale off-street parking, and Mr. Mukunda said this could make the policy extremely difficult to implement.
Leader of the Opposition R. Ashok called the policy as a “new sketch of looting government”, arguing that the proposed GBA parking rules would make residents pay ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 a year to park their cars on the road in front of their homes.
“Rows of potholes, roads that turn into swimming pools when it rains, what moral right does a government that is incapable of fixing them have to collect this parking tax?” he asked.

briefs.headline: Karnataka to introduce Command and Control Centre as part of measures to stop pilferage of PDS supplies
briefs.bodyText:
In order to prevent the pilferage of ration food grains, Karnataka is planning a seamless system including a CCTV cameras in godowns, GPS systems in vehicles that transport the PDS supplies and Command and Control Centre to monitor it all.
“The contractors concerned have been instructed to install GPS in all vehicles transporting ration grains. The Karnataka Food and Civil Supplies Corporation (KFCSC) has been instructed to install CCTVs in the KSCSC and non-KFCSC godowns. The tender process is under way to set up a Command and Control Centre in the department,” said Rizwan Arshad, Minister for Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs of Karnataka, addressing the media.
“We have technology. So why not use it,” Mr. Arshad said, adding that the new features are part of the effort to introduce a permanent solution to the problem.
Smart revamp
The department has been trying to revamp the PDS distribution through a ‘smart PDS’ system where an ePoS machine to verify the credentials of the beneficiary and an electronic weighing machine to accurately measure the quantity they are eligible for are proposed. The tender process for the installation of the same is in progress, the Minister said.
According to Mr. Arshad, as many as 1,497 FIRs have been registered in the last three years in connection with pilferage of PDS supply with 86,181 quintals of food grains and supplies worth ₹49.38 crores seized.
Deletion of BPL cards paused
As per government data, currently 4,44,32,102 beneficiaries in the State are covered under the PDS scheme.
Mr. Arshad said the Central government had provided a list of 7,76,206 people suspected to be ineligible for BPL cards. Following this, 4,26,835 ration cards have been converted into APL.
“We have stayed further deletions temporarily for now. However, as per the law we have to ultimately heed to the Central government and cannot act independently,” he said.
Regarding the Indira Food Kit scheme for the BPL card holders, the Minister noted that the department is further analysing it as the price of essentials have gone up due to the ongoing war.

stories.headline: Now, tax amnesty for undisclosed foreign assets
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: As part of efforts to get non-resident students and professionals, or those who have relocated to India, to come clean on undisclosed overseas assets and income, govt Saturday notified a new voluntary disclosure scheme for small taxpayers, who can pay an effective tax of 60% and avoid penalties and prosecution.
In a notification, govt, which had announced the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers-Disclosure Scheme in the last budget, said the scheme will open on Sunday and is due to close on Dec 31. The 
income tax department
 has fixed March 31, 2026 as the "valuation date" to compute the market value of assets that are proposed to be declared.
The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) said that the aggregate value of undisclosed foreign asset or foreign income must not exceed Rs 1 crore in case it was not previously offered to tax. Foreign assets that were already offered to tax or acquired when the taxpayer was a non-resident, but were not reported in the tax-return schedule, the threshold for declarations has been fixed at Rs 5 crore, along with a fee of Rs 1 lakh. The idea is to get someone who was a student and forgot to disclose his or her bank account details while overseas to come clean, an official said.
The undisclosed asset, including financial interest, has to be in the name of the taxpayer, including where he or she is a beneficial owner. 
Proceeds of crime or cases where assessment proceedings have been completed under the Black Money Act, 2015 are ineligible. Those availing of the scheme will have two months to pay the tax after receiving the order from authorities.
"This scheme allows taxpayers with non-disclosure of foreign income and assets, up to specified thresholds to regularise their position through a simple, one-time process. But taxpayers must note that there is a narrow window for this facility, declarations can only be filed between Aug 16, 2026 and Dec 31, 2026, with no declarations accepted thereafter. Taxpayers should evaluate eligibility and act promptly," said Richa Sawhney, tax partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, a consulting firm.

stories.headline: Government rolls out foreign asset disclosure scheme for small taxpayers
stories.deck: Taxpayers will pay a 30% tax on the value of the declared undisclosed foreign asset or income, plus an additional amount equal to the tax, effectively taking the levy to 60%
stories.bodyText:
The Income Tax Department on Saturday (August 15, 2026) notified a new voluntary disclosure scheme allowing small taxpayers to declare certain undisclosed foreign assets and income by paying an effective 60% tax, as the government seeks to bring overseas holdings into the tax net without exposing eligible taxpayers to further penalties or prosecution.
The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers-Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS), announced in the 2026-27 Budget, will take effect from Sunday (August 16, 2026), with online declarations open until December 31, 2026, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) said.
The scheme is aimed at taxpayers such as students, young professionals, technology employees and relocated non-resident Indians who may have failed to disclose eligible foreign assets or income.
Under the rules, taxpayers will pay a 30% tax on the value of the declared undisclosed foreign asset or income, plus an additional amount equal to the tax, effectively taking the levy to 60%.
The fair market value of the assets will be determined as of March 31, 2026, the CBDT said.
There are two categories of declarations under FAST-DS.
For an undisclosed foreign asset or foreign income that was not previously offered to tax, the aggregate value must not exceed ₹1 crore.
A second category covers foreign assets that were already offered to tax or acquired when the taxpayer was a non-resident but were not reported in the relevant tax-return schedule. The threshold for such declarations is ₹5 crore, with a ₹1 lakh fee payable.
The CBDT said the scheme is intended to enable eligible taxpayers to disclose "certain undisclosed foreign assets, undisclosed foreign income, or undeclared foreign assets" on payment of the specified tax or fee.
For example, where an undisclosed foreign bank account is valued at ₹60 lakh and undisclosed foreign income amounts to ₹20 lakh, the total tax payable would be ₹48 lakh, according to an example in the CBDT's frequently asked questions.
Taxpayers making valid declarations will receive immunity from any further tax or penalty and from prosecution under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, in respect of the assets or income disclosed.
The declared income or the amount invested in the disclosed asset will also not be included in the taxpayer's total income under the Income-tax Act, 1961 or the Black Money Act, the CBDT said.

stories.headline: Even as government considers MDR charge on UPI, data shows cash usage quickening in economy
stories.deck: An analysis by The Hindu shows that the growth in the value of UPI transactions has been consistently slowing since 2021-22, although the current rate of growth is still higher than that of cash with the public
stories.bodyText:
At a time when the government is proposing to allow the levy of a charge on UPI transactions, an analysis shows that the growth in the value of UPI transactions has been slowing for the last five years, while the growth of cash with the public has been quickening over this period.
Paywall: On a charge on UPI transactions
While slowing, the growth of UPI transactions remains faster than the growth of cash among the public, but this margin is shrinking. Experts say this is both a sign of higher economic activity and higher price levels than are being reflected in the official inflation data.
UPI and RuPay debit card transactions are currently free, like cash transactions. However, the government passed the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the recently-concluded Monsoon session of Parliament, which enables it to allow a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charge to be levied on these electronic transactions.
Cash is back
An analysis by The Hindu of data from the Reserve Bank of India shows that the growth rate of cash with the public reached a recent high of about 17% in the COVID-19 pandemic year of 2020-21. Thereafter, the growth of cash with the public fell consistently until 2023-24, where it hit about 4%.
Cash with the public is the total cash in circulation minus what is sitting in banks.
Since then, the growth of cash with the public has been quickening. That is, this growth rate rose to 6.5% in 2024-25 and further to 12% in 2025-26. In 2026-27, cash with the public, at ₹41.8 lakh crore as of July 31, 2026, was nearly 13% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and the Payments Corporation of India have made assurances that the general public would not have to pay the MDR charge on UPI transactions and that it would only be levied on certain high value merchants and transactions.
However, the Opposition has said that the merchants who do have to pay this charge would pass that higher cost onto their customers in the form of higher prices and that this could push people back to using cash.
UPI slowing but high
UPI transactions, on the other hand, have seen their growth slowing over the last few years, as per data with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). The value of UPI transactions conducted in the country grew 133% in 2019-20, which then slowed to a relatively robust 95% in 2020-21 as the economy locked down.
It then quickened again to 105% in 2021-22 as the economy opened up and pent-up demand combined with health fears over handling cash to push up UPI usage.
Since then, however, the growth in the value of transactions done on the UPI platform has consistently been slowing, with growth hitting 20.3% in 2025-26. In 2026-27, this has further slowed to 18.7% as of August 2026, as compared to the April-August period of last year.
However, this 18.7% growth in UPI transactions is still higher than the 13% growth in cash with the public in the same period.
Inflation likely understated
According to Pronab Sen, former Chief Statistician of India and former Chairman of the Standing Committee on Statistics, the fact that both cash and UPI are growing should be showing itself in the form of higher inflation rates than what the official numbers are currently showing.
“This would imply that we are undercounting inflation, because that’s where this should show up,” Mr. Sen told The Hindu. “If there is more money being transacted, both digitally and in cash, then that should show up in inflation. The first effect would be there.”
“A lot of this could be explained if the official data showed prices were rising faster than they are,” he added.
The latest official retail inflation data for July 2026 stood at 4.45%, slightly higher than in June, while the wholesale data showed inflation had slowed marginally to 9.8% in July from 9.9% in June.
Signs of robust economy
D.K. Srivastava, chief policy advisor at EY India, says that simultaneous cash and UPI growth is a sign of a vibrant economy.
“The first reason is increasing economic activity in general,” Mr. Srivastava said. “That is to say, high growth rates. We have been maintaining a real growth rate in excess of 7% in the post-COVID years. That is the main reason why both cash transactions and digital transactions have increased.”
Mr. Sen, however, warned that an increase in cash transactions could also point towards distress in the economy brought on by high unemployment, especially among the youth.

stories.headline: India’s forex demand shifts beyond metros as tier-2, tier-3 cities take 53% share
stories.deck: Emerging from the shadows of larger cities, smaller Indian towns now contribute to over 50% of foreign exchange demand. The appetite for leisure travel fuels this growth, with travelers aged 25 to 40 at the forefront. The US dollar continues to dominate as the most preferred currency, while digital forex transactions see a promising annual increase.
stories.bodyText:
India’s foreign exchange demand is no longer isolated in the country’s biggest cities, with smaller urban centres accounting for more than half of the total demand, according to Thomas Cook India’s Forex Report 2026.
Tier-2 and tier-3 cities together made up 53% of forex demand during the period covered by the report. Tier-2 cities alone accounted for 41%, while tier-3 cities contributed 12%. In comparison, tier-1 cities, including metros, accounted for 47%.
“Emerging India is driving the next phase of forex growth, with Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities contributing over half of overall demand,” the report said.
The data also showed that leisure travel was responsible for the largest portion of forex demand. It accounted for 57% of transactions, while corporate travel contributed 27% and student travel 16%.
According to the report, demand was spread across leisure travel, business travel and overseas education, with leisure travel remaining the dominant segment.
Travellers aged 25-40 lead demand
The 25-40 age group emerged as the largest contributor to forex usage, accounting for 37% of demand. Travellers aged 41-60 were close behind, with a 36% share.
Those aged above 60 years accounted for 21%, while the youngest category, travellers aged 18-24, represented 6% of forex demand.
“Millennials and Gen X together account for nearly three-fourths of forex usage,” the report said.
It also said senior travellers continued to make an important contribution to outbound forex demand.
Dollar accounts for nearly half of forex demand
The US dollar remained the most sought-after currency, accounting for 49% of overall forex demand.
Currencies used across Europe, represented by the euro and British pound, accounted for 23%. Asian currencies including the Thai baht, Singapore dollar, Japanese yen, Vietnamese dong and Indonesian rupiah, made up 11%.
The UAE dirham and Saudi riyal led demand from the Middle East, which accounted for 9% of the total. Australian and New Zealand currencies contributed 5%, while Canada accounted for the remaining 3%.
The report also recorded a shift towards digital forex purchases, although branch-assisted transactions remained the preferred channel, accounting for 75% of purchases.
Digital channels made up the remaining 25% of purchases. Digital forex adoption across Thomas Cook India’s channels increased 25% year-on-year, while usage of DIY platforms rose 50% year-on-year over the last two years.
The report said this reflected a gradual move towards digital-first forex transactions among Indian travellers.

briefs.headline: NCLAT upholds insolvency proceedings against Nyka Steel guarantor over UCO Bank dues
briefs.deck: Nyka Steel is already undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) before the NCLT
briefs.bodyText:
The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) has upheld an order passed by the NCLT, directing insolvency proceedings against a personal guarantor of Mumbai-based Nyka Steel.
A two-member bench of the appellate tribunal upheld a February 3, 2026 order of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Mumbai, which had admitted UCO Bank's plea to initiate insolvency proceedings against Asif Ahmed Siddique.
Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 allows creditors to start insolvency proceedings against debtors, which includes personal guarantors and partnership firms.
Nyka Steel is already undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) before the NCLT.
The petitioner had argued that no fresh deed of personal guarantee was executed for the April 12, 2018 sanction letter renewing and enhancing credit facilities to the corporate debtor, and that his guarantee covered only loans sanctioned in 2013 and 2017.
He also contended that the contractual exposure under the Deeds of Guarantee was capped at ₹40 crore and the liability of the guarantor could not have been enlarged beyond the terms of the contract.
The bank had issued demand notices in September 2023 and November 2024, raising claims of ₹51.76 crore and ₹96.23 crore, respectively.
The NCLAT, however, held that while the Deed of Guarantee dated December 12, 2017, capped the principal liability at ₹40 crore, it separately provided for interest at 12.70% per annum from the date of demand, meaning the total outstanding could exceed the capped amount.
The tribunal also noted that the petitioner had himself signed the April 2018 renewal of credit facilities, and since his 2017 guarantee was a continuing one, it could not be argued that it excluded the 2018 sanction.
Rejecting the appellant's other contentions, the NCLAT held that a lender's failure to first pursue RBI's rehabilitation framework for MSMEs does not extinguish an existing default or bar insolvency proceedings under the IBC.
It also held that the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC does not extend to personal guarantors, citing the Supreme Court's ruling in the case of State Bank of India vs V. Ramakrishnan. It said that a guarantor's liability survives even after approval of a resolution plan, per the apex court's verdict in Lalit Kumar Jain vs Union of India.
"The appeal has no merits and is accordingly dismissed without issuance of any formal notice," said the bench comprising Officiating Chairperson Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra.

briefs.headline: Tesco’s India GCC transforms from a basic dashboard to cockpit in last 20 years
briefs.deck: Its team in Bengaluru developed several AI algorithms that helped deliver around 670 million personalised offers to approximately 14-15 million customers of the British retail chain. The GCC processes payroll worth around £5.5-6 billion annually from India for the retailer’s 340,000 employees worldwide. The team connects store, customer, supply-chain, market and competition data and translates it…
briefs.bodyText:
Tesco’s India operations have evolved from a back-office support centre into a global technology and artificial intelligence hub that is increasingly helping the British retailer make decisions on sales, customer engagement, costs and operations across its nearly 5,000 stores worldwide.
The transformation can perhaps best be described as a shift from dashboards to cockpits, from merely presenting large volumes of information to giving decision-makers clear, actionable intelligence on what needs to be done. “Dashboards give a lot of information. A cockpit tells you what to do. Retail is all about execution,’’ said Venkat Raghavan, Group Director, Analytics and AI, Tesco Business Solutions, in an exclusive interview with The Hindu.
For a store manager, the difference is significant. Instead of having to sift through multiple reports, Tesco’s AI-enabled systems can flag issues such as rising theft of specific products or declining service levels, and provide the key actions required. “All stores receive this on their devices. Within five minutes they know the key actions they need to take instead of reading multiple reports,’’ Mr. Raghavan said.
The Bengaluru centre’s journey mirrors the changing role of India’s global capability centres. Tesco established its Global Capability Centre in the City in 2004, when its mandate was primarily transactional: processing payroll, supplier invoices and run customer contact centre operations for more efficiently at a lower cost.
“For the first ten years, the focus was on building trust, ensuring the work was delivered well as it had been done previously. However, over the past six-seven years, the focus has shifted significantly towards building high-end niche capabilities out of Tesco Bengaluru,’’ Mr. Raghavan explained.
The emphasis today, he said, is more on value and less on cost. In a low-margin business such as food retail, the objective is not merely to reduce operating expenses but to use technology and analytics to drive sales, improve profitability and optimise cash.
Bengaluru has consequently emerged as Tesco’s single largest software engineering hub globally and also its largest Analytics and AI hub. The India operation has around 4,000-5,000 employees, with engineering and Tesco Business Solutions teams accounting for roughly 2,500 people each. The centre also plays a significant role in Tesco’s global operations by processing payroll worth around £5.5-6 billion annually for the retailer’s 340,000 employees worldwide.
Addressing the need of the`segment of one’ through hyper-localisation
One of the most significant areas where Bengaluru is influencing Tesco’s global retail strategy is hyper-personalisation. ``Much of the thinking behind applying AI to create what we call a ‘segment of one’ came from India,’’ Mr. Raghavan said.
Retailers traditionally grouped customers into broad segments. AI is now allowing Tesco to personalise engagement at an individual level by understanding customers’ preferences, life stages and shopping journeys. Last year, the team developed several AI algorithms that helped deliver around 670 million personalised offers to approximately 14-15 million customers of Tesco globally. The offers are coordinated across the Tesco app, email and website rather than being treated as independent communications.
The capability was scaled from around one million customers to about 15 million in roughly four years through experimentation, rapid testing and learning, an approach Mr. Raghavan explained reflected India’s ability to build and scale solutions in a frugal manner.
Tesco’s long-running Clubcard loyalty programme provides a vast source of customer insight, enabling the company to understand purchasing habits, price sensitivity and life stages. However, data alone is not the differentiator for Tesco. ``Data is the foundation of everything we do. But data by itself does not create value. Value comes from the algorithms, science, and AI built on top of the data,’’ Mr. Raghavan added.
The Bengaluru team connects store, customer, supply-chain, market and competition data and translates it into decisions aimed at driving growth and profitability. The Analytics and AI organisation has now grown to around 300 data scientists and AI specialists globally, with a substantial part of the capability based in India.
AI taking position in the core of operations
According to him, the AI strategy extends beyond customer offers. Tesco is also using AI to manage costs and improve supply-chain intelligence. For instance; cost intelligence, where AI analyses the components that determine the cost of products: including raw materials, packaging, energy, freight and foreign exchange exposure, and tracks commodity movements to anticipate cost changes. The was also deploying agentic AI across core operational workflows, including invoices processing, payroll automation, customer contact centres and store property management, he said.
Tesco operates around 5,000 stores globally, each with complex infrastructure involving refrigeration, HVAC (heating ventilation and air conditioning), plumbing and safety systems. When a store reports a problem, AI can analyse the issue, identify likely root causes and route it to the appropriate vendor, he narrated.
“Over the past year we have built hundreds of such AI agents. Each agent supports core operational workflows rather than small utility functions,’’ Mr. Raghavan said. Across several workflows, agentic AI now handles around 50-60% of the effort, with humans managing exceptions. The longer-term ambition is for AI to manage processes end-to-end rather than perform isolated tasks, Mr. Raghavan added.
India becomes centre of strategic importance for Tesco
The growing importance of Bengaluru is also reflected in the level of engagement from Tesco’s global leadership. “Almost every quarter, we have at least one board director visiting this centre,’’ Mr. Raghavan said. The Chairman of the Board visited recently, while the CEO, CFO and Audit Committee leadership have also engaged with the India team.
The shift represents a fundamental change in the way Tesco views its Indian operations. ``India is no longer seen only as a cost or commercial centre. It is seen as a capability centre and as an integral part of the future of Tesco,’’ Mr. Raghavan further added.
According to Mr. Raghavan, the transformation is therefore no longer simply about a global retailer outsourcing functions to India. Bengaluru has become a place where Tesco’s technology, analytics and AI capabilities are conceived, developed and deployed globally and therefore the GCC migrating from being just a dashboard to a the cockpit which holds much of the controls of the United Kingdom-headquartered retail giant.

briefs.headline: Xiaomi bets on premium phones, connected homes as India’s smartphone market flattens
briefs.deck: The Indian smartphone industry has slightly de-grown in the first half of calendar 2026. For the second half of 2026, Xiaomi expects the market to remain broadly flat or potentially decline. Also, rising memory and storage costs still remain a pressure point for handset makers
briefs.bodyText:
Xiaomi is betting high on premium smartphones, a wider device portfolio and connected home products as India’s handset market shows clear signs of saturation, with consumers increasingly willing to spend more on devices they expect to use for longer.
The company, which has completed 12 years in India, said its Redmi Note series has crossed 85 million units shipped in the country. However, the broader smartphone industry has slightly de-grown in the first half of calendar 2026 as consumers prefer to hold on to existing devices for longer time.
With an estimated 600 million active smartphone users in India, the market was increasingly shifting from volume to value, confirmed Sandeep Sarma, Director, PR and Marketing at Xiaomi India, in a conversation with The Hindu.
“The shift is reflected in consumer spending. While the average smartphone market selling price is around ₹23,000 to ₹25,000, more consumers are moving into higher price bands. Our performance in the ₹35,000 to ₹50,000 mid-premium segment has grown 212% year-on-year,’’ he elaborated. The company has also returned to the ₹30,000 to ₹60,000 segment with the Redmi 17T and performance-focused Redmi Turbo series, both launched in June.
The solidifying trend is, consumers buying more expensive smartphones and retaining them for longer. Longer device life, combined with no-cost EMI schemes extending to 24 months—and in some cases 36 months for high-end phones—was making premium devices more accessible, he observed.
“Consumers are increasingly viewing smartphones through a monthly affordability lens rather than as a one-time purchase,’’ Mr. Sarma noted.
Battery technology was also evolving in response to longer replacement cycles, he added. ``Silicon-carbon technology was enabling smartphones to carry batteries of up to 8,000 mAh while remaining thinner and lighter, addressing the growing demand for longer battery life,’’ he explained.
At the same time, rising memory and storage costs still remain a pressure point for handset makers, with higher demand from data centres pushing up component prices.
Indian cellphone market outlook
For the second half of 2026, Xiaomi expects the Indian smartphone market to remain broadly flat or potentially decline, even through the festive season.
“Consumers are still expected to buy smartphones, but a greater share of discretionary spending could move towards televisions, tablets and other appliances,’’ he forecast.
Xiaomi will introduce Mijia, a smart home, lifestyle brand
On next phase of expansion, Mr. Sarma said, Xiaomi would introduce Mijia, Xiaomi’s smart home and lifestyle sub-brand, in India, to enter large appliances mart in India. Globally, Mijia portfolio includes air-conditioners, refrigerators and washing machines while the Chinese firm is yet to decide on product range and launch timeline for India.
“We are now focusing on this shift: from owning a smartphone as a necessity to spending on a more connected and aspirational lifestyle. Larger television screens, premium display technologies and tablets are already seeing consumers move up the price ladder, and Xiaomi expects connected home products to become the next leg of growth,’’ he added.
According to Mr. Sarma, Xiaomi’s Human x Car x Home is a smart ecosystem that links personal devices, smart home appliances, and the Xiaomi electric vehicle into one seamless software network, its operating system, Xiaomi HyperOS.
Home would be a key factor for next phase of growth for Xiaomi in India. In the first phase, the company had focused on the human part of its: human, car, home ecosystem. It sold tablets, TVs, and smartphones. In the second phase, the company will also have some smartphones and the human aspect of things, but will go more deeply into the home aspect, he added.
Explaining human, car, home ecosystem of Xiaomi Mr. Sarma said, ``You are at your office, you’re using a phone, your laptop, and your tablet, and then you go to your car, which is also a Xiaomi product. You have continuity there. You reach your home, your car talks to your home. Turn on the kettle, switch on the lights. That sort of a connected future is what we’re expecting to get in India.’’

briefs.headline: Top five big family businesses hold over 60% of income: study
briefs.bodyText:
The top five big family businesses held over 60% of income share in corporate India in the past two decades even as liberalisation made markets more competitive, according to a study appearing in World Bank Economic Review.
The study titled “Business Groups, Concentration and Market Power in India” published in the World Bank Economic Review authored by Simon Commander, visiting professor at IE Business School, Madrid, Spain among other researchers from different universities, found that Reliance, Adani, Birla, Om Prakash Jindal and Tata Groups put together controlled over 60% of business revenue between 2001 and 2020. Barring Birla Group, whose share in total gross revenue reduced steadily during the study period, the shares of other family businesses increased. Reliance and Adai Groups have consistently constituted at least 20% share in total income. The shares of Om Prakash Jindal and Tata Groups increased steadily but stayed at less than 10% of income shares.
The study acknowledges that the concentration in the market has reduced and as a result competitiveness has increased after liberalisation. This however has not prevented the large family business groups from dominating the market. The top 25 family business groups constitute over 15% of the Gross Domestic Product–the value of goods and services sold–in 2020, the study observed.
“The paper finds that market concentration has indeed been declining during that period, mainly due to policy-induced shrinkage of the public sector. Concentration has also been falling for the private sector and for the FBGsThus, at the NIC-3 level, the proportion of industries with low concentration has risen considerably over the period,” the authors observed. The largest five firms controlled more than half of the revenues in around 74 percent of NIC-3 industries, the study found. NIC 3 refers to a Statistics Ministry classification of industries by specific subsectors.
At the same time, family business groups have also diversified across different sectors, the study found.
The authors concluded that Indian government’s approach of showing preference for some business groups as “national champions” in the period between 2000 and 2013 may have led to the higher concentration.
“To date, public policy appears to have achieved, at best, limited success in addressing the consequences of this increased concentration for competition, whether in terms of market power in specific sectors or with respect to the level of overall concentration in the economy,” the authors wrote.
Competition policy, taxation or prohibitions will not be as effective in addressing entrenched family business group power in Indian market, the authors said while suggesting that setting specific limits to the maximum market share that a business group can hold and a subsequently divesting when a specified level is reached can be explored as a policy option.

briefs.headline: IT rights body writes to Labour Ministry over Wipro’s onboarding delays
briefs.deck: The affected candidates were selected through Wipro’s Elite Hiring 2025 process
briefs.bodyText:
The Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES), a Mumbai-based organisation working for the rights of IT employees, has sent a written complaint to Union Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya regarding the “prolonged and unexplained delay” in onboarding more than 200 students and young engineers selected by Wipro Limited under its Elite Hiring 2025 process.
Harpreet Singh Saluja, president of NITES and an advocate of the Bombay High Court, stated in the letter that the affected students and young engineers participated in Wipro’s campus recruitment process on February 1, 2025, and cleared subsequent rounds in the same month. Following their interviews, they received their offer letters on July 22, 2025, and ‘Letters of Intent’ in August 2025.
“In December 2025, they reconfirmed their interest through Wipro’s official survey,” Mr. Saluja said, adding that despite completing every requirement communicated by Wipro, these students and young engineers have still not received a definite onboarding or joining date.
“For several months, the affected students and young engineers have repeatedly approached Wipro HR, onboarding helpdesks and other designated channels but state that they have received no substantive response,” the letter read.
Wipro’s response
A Wipro spokesperson told The Hindu that Wipro remains committed to onboarding the freshers, in line with its business requirements. “We will continue to keep candidates informed on further updates,” the spokesperson added.
Mr. Saluja said educational institutions and Training and Placement Officers of the students also attempted to obtain clarification from Wipro’s campus relationship personnel, without satisfactory resolution.
“The consequences are serious. These are young people at the beginning of their professional careers who planned their careers and financial commitments around the employment opportunity offered by Wipro. Many state that they declined or did not pursue other employment opportunities while awaiting onboarding. They and their families have consequently faced continuing financial uncertainty and burdens relating to education, accommodation, daily expenses and family responsibilities. The prolonged uncertainty has also caused considerable anxiety, frustration and emotional distress and has prevented students from taking informed decisions regarding alternative employment and further education,” the letter said.
Mr. Saluja urged the Minister to treat the complaint as urgent and initiate appropriate action at the earliest.
