briefs.headline: What is the latest Mining Amendment Act about? | Explained
briefs.deck: The opposition to the proposed act primarily centres on a potential subversion to the federal structure of how revenue from mining resources is taxed, especially in resource-rich and States which particularly depend on taxing the resources for revenue.
briefs.bodyText:
The story so far: The Rajya Sabha on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) passed an amendment to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, which, among other things, specifies that States do not levy any tax or cess on mineral, mineral bearing lands and overall operations. The now-ratified legislation has drawn immense opposition from several mineral-rich States, including Odisha and Jharkhand – accusing the Union Govt of encroaching upon their constitutional powers.
What does the law primarily entail?
With an objective to impart “stability, certainty and predictability” into the fiscal regime of the mineral sector, the ratified legislation, among other things, seeks that State governments do not impose any tax, cess or similar levies centred around mineral rights.
This primarily seeks to avert instances of price arbitrage for the same mineral across States and bring about equitable price regime. For context, Tamil Nadu and Jharkhand had instituted mineral-bearing land (MBL) tax on various mineral in 2024 and 2025 respectively. In Tamil Nadu, the tax was fixed at ₹160 per metric tonne.
Jharkhand had introduced the tax at ₹100 per metric tonne although it was hiked across multiple tranches.
The introduction of the taxation in Tamil Nadu cast apprehensions among cement producers in the State. They indicated that the elevated price of the primary raw material, that is, limestone, would have to be ultimately passed on to the consumers, thus elevating the retail prices of cement.
Similar concerns erupted in Jharkhand for coal and bauxite.
According to the Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI), the amendment would provide greater certainty and stability in the fiscal framework for mining.
“This should help improve investor confidence and encourage investment in exploration, mine development and expansion of existing mines, which can support higher domestic production and better availability of minerals,” the industry group told The Hindu.
The now-ratified law takes retrospective effect, in other words, any such levy liable but not collected before the legislation is formally enforced would be deemed invalid.
What has been the opposition to the proposed legislation?
The opposition to the proposed act primarily centres on a potential subversion to the federal structure of how revenue from mining resources is taxed, especially in resource-rich and States which particularly depend on taxing the resources for revenue.
According to a report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CGI), about 41.4% of a State’s non-tax revenues came from mineral and petroleum related receipts combined.
Naveen Patnaik, former Chief Minister of Odisha and president of the Biju Janata Dal (BJD) said the Bill impinges upon the State’s fiscal autonomy and threatened its constitutional rights over its resources.
In a letter to the incumbent Chief Minister, he said the provisions would “disproportionately impact” mineral-rich States such as Odisha, leading to “massive revenue losses” and stifling the State’s developmental agenda.
Hemant Soren, Chief Minister of Jharkhand, termed the provisions of the law to be according “stepmotherly treatment”.
“In Jharkhand, schemes providing social security to millions – such as the Maiya Samman Yojana, Abua Awas Yojana, pensions, education, health, and others – will be on the verge of closure,” he pointed out.
Further, V.D. Satheesan, Chief Minister of Kerala has sought to mount a strong political opposition, and if required, legal opposition to the Act.
What has been the Union Govt’s response?
Speaking to the press on Thursday (August 13), G. Kishan Reddy, Union Minister for Coal and Mines refuted assertions about the ratified law seeking to impinge upon the right of States over their resources.
He argued the legislation is primarily aimed at ensuring growth and equitability in the overall ecosystem.
Also Read : Documents show Modi government pushed coal reforms despite internal criticism, benefiting major mining firms
“The government’s primary objective is to ensure identical [taxation] rates across the board to ensure [effective prices] do not spike. We are neither seeking to impinge upon any State’s rights nor acquire any control [over States’ resources],” he stated.
Further, the Minister said the amendment encompasses only certain major minerals and does not extend to minor minerals over which the States retain absolute control.
He put forth the minerals are critical to infrastructure, manufacturing, energy security and overall economic development.
Thus, the focus on ensuring price equitability and better economics.
According to a memo circulated by the government, the list of major minerals includes coal, lignite, iron ore, graphite, cobalt, lithium and nickel among others.
Moreover, the legislative regime would encompass across eleven states only, including Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Goa.
Furthermore, Mr. Reddy, arguing the Centre also ensured flow of revenue to States, reported that States’ share in overall mineral revenues have accelerated from 65% to 88% between fiscal year 2014-15 and 2024-25, while the share from coal rose to 96% from 55% during the same period.

briefs.headline: Smartphone to be locked for missed EMI? RBI’s new rules for lenders, defaulting borrowers explained
briefs.deck: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has laid out some guidelines for lenders on recovery of loans, and whether they can block or lock the device that has been purchased via EMI financing. This new framework will come into effect from January 1, 2027.
briefs.bodyText:
Purchased a smartphone, laptop or tablet via loan financing? What happens if you miss an EMI? Can the lender lock your phone or block access to the device? According to a study by Home Credit Finance, the single biggest reason for borrowing in 2025 remained the purchase of smartphones and home appliances.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has laid out some guidelines for lenders on recovery of loans, and whether they can block or lock the device that has been purchased via EMI financing. This new framework will come into effect from January 1, 2027.
The new framework governing loan recovery practices comes on the back of increasing complaints from borrowers who have alleged harassment in the recovery process. This harassment has in the past taken the form of intimidation through social media and also the use of abusive language.
In 2024, RBI asked lenders to stop the practice of locking phones of borrowers in case of default. Lenders were doing this using an app that was installed at the time of the loan issuance.
In May this year, the RBI had released a draft framework that outlined proposed norms on the "Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents". The central bank had invited comments from stakeholders. 
The final norms have now been released.
What do the new rules mean for you? What are your rights as a borrower and what does a loan default for EMI-financed devices mean for you? We break it down:
RBI’s new rules: Can your phone be locked?
RBI has clearly told lenders that they cannot disable the borrower’s mobile phone, laptop or tablet in cases of loans taken for home, car or other personal loans. The restrictions to use can only come in place for devices that have been financed via loans.
"A bank shall not deploy any technology-based mechanism...which restricts or disables any of the functionalities of a mobile device of a borrower such as mobile phone, tablet and laptop as a recovery tool, except to recover its loan dues arising out from financing of such a device," RBI has said.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: What Lenders Can Do
Even in such cases the restrictions have to be gradual and with certain rules in place. Let’s take a look at what the lender can and can’t do:
What the lender can do:
Lenders have been allowed to impose gradual restrictions on the devices after 30 days of the payment being overdue.
So, to begin with if your EMI is overdue for less than 30 days then the lender cannot do anything to the device. The lender is required to send you a formal notice.
If the loan remains overdue between 30-60 days, then the gradual restrictions can be introduced.
The full contractual restrictions can only be imposed after the loan has been overdue for more than 60 days.
If a device locking software is eventually used, it can only be one that is certified by the original equipment manufacturer or the operating system provider.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: What Lenders Can't Do
But outgoing and incoming calls cannot be stopped.
SMS, Emergency SOS and any restrictions that impact work or employment are not allowed.
Lenders cannot access details on the borrower's phone such as contacts, photos, call logs, location history or even SMSes.
Borrowers should also be aware that once the loan payment is received by the lender, the device has to be unlocked within an hour. Any delay in unlocking at the lender’s end will entail a Rs 250 per hour compensation for the borrower, up to the loan amount.
Additionally, no uncertified recovery agents will be allowed to interact with the borrowers for the loan.
What do the new rules mean for you?
The biggest takeaway for loan borrowers is that your device can’t be blocked for non-payment of EMIs. Also, if at all any restrictions come into place, they can only be if the loan has financed that particular device. The loan agreement needs to clearly state these conditions.
“A missed EMI can no longer make your phone go dark. From 1 January 2027, the default is that lenders cannot lock or disable a device to recover dues at all. The sole exception is a device bought on that specific loan, and only if the agreement says so, notice is given, and functionality is curbed gradually. A defaulted car loan, personal loan or credit card can never touch your phone,” explains Vivek Iyer, Partner and Financial Services Risk Advisory Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: Know Borrower Rights
So the next important thing to note is this: always read the terms and conditions of the loan agreement when opting for an EMI-financed device.
“Read the agreement for how it treats remote access and default remedies. The restriction is unenforceable unless written in expressly. Borrow only from regulated lenders, since every safeguard depends on it,” Vivek Iyer recommends.
“Set up auto-debit, because 30 days now starts a formal pathway. And insist on written notice. That is your evidence for both the graded-step rule and any compensation claim,” Iyer adds.
According to Adhil Shetty, CEO of Bankbazaar.com, the new framework brings greater clarity to how lenders can use technology for recovery of dues on EMI-financed purchases.
“It allows action against genuine defaults while placing clearer limits on how that action can be taken. A key safeguard is that a lender cannot restrict a device that was not financed through the loan. For borrowers, the broader impact is greater clarity around their rights and privacy. This should create a better balance between a lender's need to recover dues and a borrower's right to fair treatment,” he tells TOI.
The Bankbazaar CEO also advocates carefully reading the term agreements instead of just focusing on the monthly EMI figure.
Why India borrowed in 2025 (Source: Home Credit Finance Report)
“Consumers should look beyond the monthly EMI and understand the financing terms before committing to a purchase. They should check whether the agreement allows device-based recovery and understand the consequences of missing payments,” he tells TOI.
Yet another important point to note is that while the RBI’s rules safeguard the privacy and rights of individuals, they do not remove the repayment obligation.
“The EMI should therefore be comfortably affordable and the recovery terms understood before taking the loan,” Shetty says.
Some steps also need attention after you have repaid the loan.
Santosh Agarwal, CEO of Paisabazaar suggests that on successful repayment of the loan, borrowers should get the access relinquished and disable any technology mechanism at the earliest.
“It is important for borrowers to retain all repayment proof and contact the lender for unlocking their devices,” she tells TOI.

briefs.headline: Anthropic's IPO may hinge on a $200 billion revenue bet: Here's what investors are looking at
briefs.deck: Anthropic forecasts remarkable revenue growth by the year 2028, with projections estimating earnings reaching between $190 billion and $200 billion. Investors closely analyze other tech companies like Palantir and SpaceX in light of these figures. However, Anthropic's current expenditures are straining profit margins, necessitating greater operational efficiency and scalability to enhance its…
briefs.bodyText:
Anthropic is preparing for what could become one of the world’s biggest IPOs, with investors and bankers looking beyond the AI firm’s current performance and towards 2028 to assess how much the company could be worth.
Two people familiar with Anthropic's financials portfolio told Reuters that the company is forecasting revenue of about $190 billion to $200 billion in 2028. That estimate is far above the $47 billion revenue run rate the company disclosed in May, underlining the extent of the expansion being factored into its prospective valuation.
Bankers and investors are applying enterprise value-to-revenue multiples to projected figures. Such multiples are widely used for fast-growing software companies that have not yet reached a mature profit profile.
Using estimates two years into the future, however, is less usual. People familiar with the process said this reflects both the speed of Anthropic's expansion and the difficulty of finding appropriate benchmarks for a company still committing large sums to AI infrastructure.
Anthropic's spending on computing capacity, model training and hiring is putting pressure on its margins. 
The scale of AI investment has also contributed to recent pullbacks in several highly valued technology stocks, including some companies considered comparable to Anthropic.
Still, other fast-growing companies have used longer-term projections in their path to public markets. Backers of Cerebras Systems pointed to 2028 revenue expectations before its IPO this year, while SpaceX's projections went as far as 2029 before it went public at a record valuation in June, the people said.
Palantir, Cloudflare and SpaceX in focus
Investors are looking at a range of companies to establish a valuation framework for Anthropic ahead of its analyst day. The list includes cloud infrastructure company Cloudflare, enterprise software company Palantir and SpaceX, according to the people.
Comparable companies are a key part of IPO pricing because they provide a reference for how businesses with similar growth rates or models are valued. They can also help investors decide which revenue or earnings multiples to apply to financial forecasts.
Palantir is valued at 53 times its expected revenue for this year, while SpaceX and Cloudflare are each trading at 41.6 times expected 2026 revenue, according to LSEG data.
The three companies provide different reference points. Palantir is used by investors as a benchmark for rapidly expanding businesses with AI exposure. Cloudflare offers a comparison with a high-growth software and infrastructure company. SpaceX, meanwhile, demonstrates how expectations around future scale can form part of a company's valuation even when current financial performance is not the primary basis.
Current spending clouds the profit picture
Anthropic's present earnings do not necessarily show the economics investors expect from the company once it reaches greater scale.
The company is spending heavily on GPUs and other computing capacity, model training, inference and recruitment. While these costs are supporting its expansion, investors expect them to decline as a proportion of revenue as the business grows.
The change in Anthropic's revenue run rate has been rapid. It stood at about $9 billion at the end of 2025 and had climbed above $47 billion by May, Reuters reported.
For the second quarter of 2026, Anthropic has projected revenue of at least $10.9 billion, more than twice the previous quarter. It is also on track to report its first quarterly operating profit, at $559 million.
The company has said its revenue run rate increased more than 10-fold annually in each of the three years through early 2026.
That growth is central to the decision to use 2028 projections in assessing the company's valuation. Investors are effectively betting that the money Anthropic is spending now will support much larger revenue and improved margins later.
The company could also see greater efficiency in training and inference as technology develops, while personnel and other operating costs could make up a smaller portion of revenue as the business expands.

stories.headline: 'I now know I was wrong': Hikaru on chaotic EWC match against Firouzja
stories.deck: Hikaru Nakamura finished third at the 2026 Esports World Cup after Alireza Firouzja forfeited their match following technical issues and multiple disconnections. Initially blaming chess.com, Nakamura later learned the problems were caused by the EWC. He apologised for his comments, admitted he jumped to conclusions, and earned $145,000 plus valuable Club Championship points for Falcons Esports.
stories.bodyText:
Grandmaster Hikaru Nakamura has explained what happened during his chaotic third-place match against Alireza Firouzja at the Esports World Cup 2026, after a series of technical problems eventually brought the contest to an unexpected end.
Nakamura was competing against his Falcons Esports teammate Firouzja for third place. The match was already close and complicated when multiple players experienced disconnections.
Another game was affected by the technical problems, and Firouzja eventually left the match.
Multiple disconnections cause chaos and controversy
Nakamura said he was left waiting for around 20 minutes before officials told him that the match would be recorded as a forfeit in his favour. At the time, however, he did not know what had caused the problem.
“Today's match with Alireza certainly didn't go well for anyone. It was chaos with multiple disconnections and then Alireza's untimely departure from the event,” Nakamura explained in an official statement.
The American grandmaster said he had no access to his phone or outside information while waiting. Because the first thing he saw on his screen was a disconnection, he assumed the problem was with chess.com.
After the forfeit was confirmed, Nakamura was taken to do interviews. Still frustrated and without the full context, he publicly said that he believed chess.com was responsible.
Nakamura retracts his comments
He has since admitted that assumption was incorrect.
“I now know I was wrong. It was an EWC issue that took out a few events, not just chess,” Nakamura said. He added that he wished he had been given that information before doing the interviews, saying that he had “jumped to conclusions” and wrongly blamed chess.com.
Nakamura apologised to chess.com and asked for his retraction to be shared wherever his original comments had appeared. He also jokingly dismissed suggestions that he had been pressured into changing his story, saying he was “not under duress by the ‘chess mafia’” and that Danny was not “holding my hand on the stove.”
Despite the dramatic ending, Nakamura officially finished third at the Esports World Cup, defeating Firouzja after leading 3-1 with two games remaining before the forfeit. The result earned him $145,000 and valuable Club Championship points for Falcons Esports.

stories.headline: Flashback: What happened when India last hosted BWF World Championships
stories.deck: New Delhi is set to welcome the prestigious 2026 Badminton World Championships after a long hiatus of seventeen years. The last event in 2009 in Hyderabad witnessed China's commanding presence, highlighted by Lin Dan's monumental victory. With the stakes higher than ever, India prepares to write a new chapter in this thrilling sport, reflecting the dramatic shifts in international badminton.
stories.bodyText:
Seventeen years after Hyderabad hosted the 
BWF World Championships
, badminton's biggest tournament is returning to India with the 2026 edition set to begin at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi. The return offers an opportunity to look back at the last time the world's best shuttlers gathered in India — an edition remembered for China's extraordinary dominance, Lin Dan's historic triumph and one of the greatest men's doubles finals in World Championships history.
Hyderabad 2009 was very much the era of the Chinese juggernaut. China won four of the five gold medals on offer, with Denmark's Thomas Laybourn and Kamilla Rytter Juhl providing the only interruption to their sweep by winning the mixed doubles title.
The competitive landscape, however, has changed significantly since then. Three of the five finals in Hyderabad featured players or pairs from the same country, whereas only one of the 25 finals across the last five editions has been an all-same-country affair.
Lin Dan completed historic hat-trick
The men's singles title in Hyderabad cemented Lin Dan's status as one of badminton's greats. The Chinese star arrived as a two-time world champion and left with a third title, having dropped only one game throughout the tournament.
Lin's path included the unexpected quarterfinal exit of Lee Chong Wei, who lost to Indonesia's Sony Dwi Kuncoro. Two-time champion Taufik Hidayat reached the semifinals but was comfortably beaten by China's Chen Jin, while Lin defeated Chen in the final to add another world title to the Olympic gold he had won in Beijing the previous year.
China also dominated the women's events. Lu Lan defeated two-time champion Xie Xingfang in the women's singles final, while Zhang Yawen and Zhao Tingting claimed their first world title in women's doubles.
A final for the ages in men's doubles
The tournament's most memorable contest came in men's doubles, where Cai Yun and Fu Haifeng faced South Korea's Jung Jae Sung and Lee Yong Dae.
The Chinese pair eventually prevailed 28-26, winning an extraordinary 75-minute final that has since been regarded as one of the greatest men's doubles matches played at the World Championships.
That victory gave China its fourth gold of the tournament and provided a dramatic finale to an event that had produced compelling action throughout the week.
17 years later, a different badminton landscape
The 2009 championships began amid concerns over a bird-flu outbreak in Asia, but those worries quickly faded once the competition got underway. Seventeen years later, the tournament returns to India in a considerably more competitive badminton landscape.
The Chinese dominance that defined Hyderabad continued for a few more years but has not been replicated by any nation since 2012. That expanded competitive field will be on display in New Delhi, with the world's leading players arriving with ambitions of winning the world title.
The venue itself has also undergone a major transformation ahead of the tournament. More than Rs 20 crore has reportedly been spent on refurbishing the stadium following concerns raised during the India Open earlier this year, which served as a test event.
With players already training at the revamped stadium, attention now shifts to whether India's return as World Championships hosts can produce another memorable chapter.

briefs.headline: Tamil Nadu Premier League | Sachin, Jhathavedh help Kings end three-game losing streak
briefs.bodyText:
A special occasion demanded special performances.
In the 100th Tamil Nadu Premier League match hosted at the NPR College ground here, top-order batter B. Sachin (77, 45b, 6x4, 4x6) and leg-spinner Jhathavedh Subramanyan (4-0-10-3) joined the party as Vida Kovai Kings thumped Trichy Grand Cholas by 116 runs on Saturday.
Chasing 202, Grand Cholas were jolted early as medium-pacer Deeban Lingesh sent back skipper-opener J. Suresh Kumar for a duck in the first over. Left-arm spinner M. Siddharth dismissed Shyam Sundar, the centurion from the previous game, before Deeban returned to castle J. Kousik.
Kovai Kings went from strength to strength, with Jhathavedh disturbing Bhavan Suriya’s furniture to leave Grand Cholas reeling at 40 for four in the daunting chase.
Opener K. Rajkumar (32) was handed a reprieve in the eighth over when C. Andre Siddarth put him down at long-on off Prashid Akash. The debutant, however, found joy as he ended Jafar Jamal’s stay soon after.
Jhathavedh came back to remove K. Rajkumar, who could not capitalise on his ‘life’, and Antony Dhas to have the Trichy outfit staring down the barrel at 59 for seven.
R.S. Ambrish soon joined in the celebration, dismissing R. Rajkumar and Ganesh Moorthi as Shahrukh Khan’s Kovai Kings finally broke free of their three-match losing streak. Earlier, after the Kovai side was asked to bat, Sachin held the innings together while finding an able ally in Madhava Prasad (38 n.o.). The pair added 75 off 43 balls for the sixth wicket as Kovai Kings went past the 200-mark.

briefs.headline: DPL | Tejasvi shines in Superstarz’s win
briefs.deck: Tejasvi’s 29-ball 60 paved the way for Superstarz to knock off a target of 218 with two balls to spare
briefs.bodyText:

briefs.headline: Badminton World championships | India’s home-court intensity the talking point at the Worlds
briefs.bodyText:
The badminton World championships will begin here on Monday, with the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium already buzzing with activity as players sweated it out in their final practice sessions.
The tournament, which runs until August 23, marks the return of the event to India for the first time since 2009.
“I feel like the drift… the weather, everything is very well maintained and very good as compared to last time,” said World No. 2 Wang Zhiyi. She added that the focus over the last few days had been on training rather than obsessing over opponents.
Former Olympic champion Chen Yufei was still not fully fit after retiring injured against P.V. Sindhu at the Japan Open, allowing the Indian to reach her first final in more than two years. “It’s better than the last match but I think it’s not 100%,” she said.
Chen played down preparing for any one rival, saying she would focus on each match. That approach could be tested later in the tournament against An Se-young, with whom she has been battling since 2018. The head-to-head is 14-17 now. Sindhu has also proved a particularly difficult opponent for Chinese players at the World championships.
Liang Weikeng and Wang Chang are still chasing their first crown, having won bronze in 2023. They spoke of the importance of playing together, saying they “motivate each other” and quickly move on after mistakes.
Their history with Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty makes the potential quarterfinal intriguing. The Liang-Wang duo had won four straight times against them before the Indians finally won in Paris last year, only for the Chinese pair to respond with a victory at the World Tour Finals.
On the practice courts, the intensity was evident. Sat-Chi sparred with M.R. Arjun and Hariharan Amsakarunan while Tanisha Crasto and Dhruv Kapila trained alongside Rohan Kapoor and Ruthvika Gadde. Sindhu and Ayush Shetty traded attacking exchanges, with coach Irwansyah Adi Pratama watching on.

briefs.headline: Ferran Torres trains with PSG for the first time after 2031 deal
briefs.deck: Ferran Torres has joined Paris Saint-Germain from Barcelona for a reported €50 million, signing until 2031 just weeks after scoring Spain’s World Cup-winning goal against Argentina. The 26-year-old will wear PSG’s No. 9 shirt and reunite with Luis Enrique, arriving after a productive Barcelona campaign that saw him score 21 goals across all competitions.
briefs.bodyText:
Ferran Torres has begun life at Paris Saint-Germain, joining his new team-mates in training for the first time after completing his move from Barcelona. The Spain international was pictured in PSG training kit on Saturday, shortly after his transfer to the reigning European champions was made official, beginning a new chapter alongside some of Europe's most prominent attacking players.
PSG move for World Cup final hero
Torres' move to Paris Saint-Germain was made official on Saturday morning, according to L'Équipe, with the 26-year-old subsequently joining his new team-mates for training later in the day.
PSG's social-media channels published the first photographs of the forward with the squad, showing Torres working alongside his new team-mates and receiving a traditional guard of honour as he was welcomed into the group.
The Spain international has signed a contract running until 2031 after PSG agreed a reported €50 million ($58.5 million) deal with Barcelona. He will wear the No. 9 shirt in Paris.
Torres arrived in the French capital after passing his medical and completing the formalities of the transfer, having only recently written his name into World Cup history with Spain.
The move also brings Torres back together with Luis Enrique, who played an influential role in his Spain career and has been a major force behind his arrival in Paris.
Torres arrives after a particularly productive final season at Barcelona, scoring 21 goals and providing three assists in 49 appearances in all competitions as the Catalan club retained their LaLiga title.
The goal that changed his summer
Torres' value rose sharply during Spain's World Cup campaign, with his defining moment coming in the final against Argentina.
With the match still level after 90 minutes, Torres scored in extra time to give Spain a 1-0 victory and the World Cup. Argentina finished as runners-up, while Torres left the tournament as the player responsible for its decisive moment.
Spain's Ferran Torres celebrates with the trophy after winning the World Cup final soccer match between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, N.J., near New York, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Ashley Landis)
That goal came six weeks before his move to Paris and helped transform the perception around a forward who had often been productive at Barcelona without becoming an undisputed first-choice star.
PSG's decision to move quickly for him reflects the opportunity created by that rise. The Champions League holders have not simply added a player coming off a strong domestic season; they have signed a World Cup-winning forward whose most important contribution came on the biggest stage.
What Torres brings to PSG
Torres gives Luis Enrique another forward capable of operating in several positions.
He has played as a winger and central striker during spells with Manchester City and Barcelona, allowing him to move between the flanks and the centre depending on the tactical demands of a match.
That flexibility is particularly relevant at PSG, where Enrique has built an attack based on pressing, movement and players capable of exchanging positions.
Torres will now compete for minutes alongside Ousmane Dembélé, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Désiré Doué and Bradley Barcola, giving Enrique another versatile option across the front line.
His previous relationship with Enrique is another factor in the move. The pair worked together with Spain, and they will now resume that partnership at club level in Paris.
For PSG, the €50m investment also represents a long-term commitment. His contract runs until 2031, while the No. 9 shirt places him in a prominent attacking role at a club that has just won the Champions League.
The challenge will now be translating his World Cup form into a new league and a new dressing room, with PSG expecting Torres to contribute immediately while also developing into a long-term part of the squad.
From Valencia to Manchester City and Barcelona
Torres began his senior career at Valencia, making his first-team debut in 2017 after progressing through the club's academy.
Manchester City signed him in August 2020 in a reported €23m deal, and he quickly added major honours to his CV. During his time under Pep Guardiola, he won the 
Premier League
 and EFL Cup in the 2020-21 season.
Barcelona brought him back to Spain in 2022, where he developed into a versatile forward capable of contributing from both wide positions and through the middle.
Across 207 appearances for Barcelona, Torres scored 65 goals and collected six major honours, including three LaLiga titles, three Spanish Super Cups and a Copa del Rey. He had also won the Premier League and EFL Cup with Manchester City.
His Barcelona career was therefore defined less by being the club's unquestioned attacking focal point and more by consistent production across several positions.
Now, after four years in Catalonia and a World Cup-winning goal for Spain, Torres begins the next stage of his career in Paris. PSG have handed him a contract through 2031 and the No. 9 shirt, with the reigning European champions hoping the forward who decided the World Cup final can become an important figure in their pursuit of more silverware.

briefs.headline: ‘We will try not to make mistakes’: Harmanpreet vows India will learn from Wales win
briefs.deck: India marked a stellar opening in the Hockey World Cup, defeating Wales 3-1. Harmanpreet Singh, the captain, shined with two penalty corner goals. Despite a late strike from Wales, which highlighted room for growth, the Indian forward line proved effective, earning numerous penalty corners. With such a performance, the squad is confident in their quest for a medal in the tournament.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India captain 
Harmanpreet Singh
 was pleased with his side's winning start to the FIH Hockey World Cup but admitted there were lessons to take from the 3-1 victory over Wales in their Pool D opener in Amstelveen on Saturday. Harmanpreet, who scored twice from penalty corners, said securing the full three points was the immediate priority, while stressing that India would look to avoid repeating the mistakes that allowed Wales to score late in the contest.
“We played very well. Our aim was to create chances and score goals match after match. It doesn't matter who is the man of the match or who is scoring the goals. We just need to score goals. We played with that mindset,” Harmanpreet said after the match.
“It was important to begin with a good win. We won 3-1 and took three points, which is a good result,” he added.
India look to tighten up after late Wales goal
India had established a commanding 3-0 advantage by the 43rd minute, with Sanjay opening the scoring in the eighth minute before Harmanpreet struck in the 11th and 43rd minutes. However, Wales managed to pull one back in the 56th minute after a scramble inside the Indian goalmouth, denying the former champions a clean sheet.
Harmanpreet acknowledged the need for India to learn from the lapse as they move deeper into the tournament.
“We tried our best, but they also played well. This was only the first match, and we will try not to make mistakes in future matches,” said the India captain.
The goal came after a lengthy deliberation following an unusual sequence in which the referee dropped his whistle while trying to retrieve it and missed part of the action. A review by the third umpire eventually confirmed Sam Welsh's goal, reducing the deficit to 1-3.
Penalty corners deliver, confidence remains high
All three of India's goals came from penalty corners, with Sanjay and Harmanpreet making the most of their drag-flick opportunities. Despite coach Craig Fulton's emphasis on improving India's field-goal conversion, Harmanpreet said the source of the goals mattered less than the end result.
“Our forward line performed well and earned several penalty corners. Whether they score field goals or create PCs, goals are important for the team,” he said.
India had largely controlled the contest, particularly in the first quarter, when they established their 2-0 advantage. Wales offered greater resistance after the break, but Harmanpreet's second goal in the 43rd minute gave India enough cushion to manage the final stages.
The captain also expressed confidence in the team's preparation and current form after a mixed run in the build-up to the World Cup.
“Currently, the team's focus is on the World Cup and we are in good form, well prepared, and confident of a podium finish,” he said.
India will now turn their attention to England, whom they face in their second Pool D match on Monday. The contest is scheduled to begin at 6:30 PM IST.

briefs.headline: Badminton World championships | China no longer the predominant force in racquet sport
briefs.deck: China has three women in the top 10 but only two more in top 100. The men fare better, numerically; six in top 50 and eight in top 100.
briefs.bodyText:
The Chinese aura is diminishing.
For a formidable machine that churned out winners like clockwork and has had an incredible 72 champions, Shi Yuqi is the only one who will go into the upcoming badminton World championships looking to defend his title.
Shi’s win in Paris last year ended a 10-year barren streak, the previous winner being Chen Long in 2015.
Among the women, the drought has been much longer. Yihan Wang was the last Chinese to win the title way back in 2011. No wonder, most of the queries to the ones here revolved around the pressure of expectations.
“The players of China are very good and large in number. We don’t have pressure of performance as such; it is more about learning from each other and it benefits everyone,” World No. 9 Li Shifeng said on Saturday.
It’s a recurrent theme — the power of numbers, the insistence on lack of pressure and self-belief. But there is no denying the fact that the rest of the world has successfully ended the Chinese chokehold on the sport.
Consider this: China has three women in the top 10 but only two more in top 100. The men fare better, numerically; six in top 50 and eight in top 100.
Chen Yufei has come the closest to breaking the jinx, reaching the World championships finals in two of the last three editions but going down to Akane Yamaguchi both times, including last year. Her most recent outing, at the China Open, again ended in a straight games loss to Yamaguchi.
“I think it is more about ourselves, how we prepare. There is no pressure, only an expectation to do our best. You just need to have faith in yourself and not care about anything else. My biggest obstacle is myself and if I can conquer that, I believe I can win gold,” Yufei said about the missing title in her cabinet.
The red shirts on court are always intimidating. For now, though, the pressure is on them.

briefs.headline: IND vs SL Test Day 1: The way Padikkal played was really encouraging, says Kotak
briefs.deck: I would look at the way they bat, about how they are adapting to conditions, how they are dealing with the different stages, says Sitanshu Kotak
briefs.bodyText:
Hopping across the Palk Strait, Devdutt Padikkal has found his groove. In the warm-up fixture in Colombo, he cracked an unbeaten 142, and once he moved to Sri Lanka’s southern coast, a splendid maiden Test hundred was essayed. “I am so happy for him. He was waiting for this opportunity and the way he played was really encouraging,” India’s batting coach Sitanshu Kotak said.
Talking to the media after the conclusion of the first Test’s opening day in Galle on Saturday (August 16, 2026), Kotak offered his appraisal of Padikkal: “When I was at the NCA, he was working on his initial movement; he also worked on his back foot game. When we expect there will be turn, we try and work on stepping-out, sweep or back-foot game. A lot of credit goes to him.”
Asked specifically if Padikkal’s ton has erased India’s worries over the number three slot, Kotak said: “He batted well; Sai (Sudarshan) too has batted well at that number. But the thing is, they are all new batters. We are flexible in a way. Mainly, I would look at the way they bat, about how they are adapting to conditions, how they are dealing with the different stages. How they bat is important to me more than the number they bat at.”
Kotak termed the pitch as dry and explained: “When we saw the wicket, we felt that it is on the drier side. And there is no doubt that it is on the drier side. 288 for two is a good sign for us but it is just one day and we have a long way to go. I don’t think it will crack but I think it will spin more as the game progresses. The overall record shows that as the game progresses (at Galle), the average return of the batters goes down noticeably.”
K.L. Rahul’s adaptability was also lauded and Kotak said: “In Tests he opens, in limited overs cricket he comes in at five or six. He is flexible that way and in a young team when a senior like him plays well, it always helps. He takes responsibility, builds partnerships and is consistent.”
And as for Yashasvi Jaiswal’s run out, Kotak clarified: “It is just that KL stopped halfway. Jaiswal got up and took one step. And that’s why probably that misunderstanding happened. But these things happen and it is unfortunate.”

briefs.headline: ‘The way he has prepared’: India coach explains key to Padikkal’s maiden century
briefs.deck: Devdutt Padikkal scored an unbeaten 131 on his maiden international century. His improved back-foot game was credited by batting coach Sitanshu Kotak. Padikkal adapted well to Sri Lanka's spin-heavy bowling attack. KL Rahul also contributed significantly before retiring hurt from the match. Sri Lanka's coach praised both Indian batters for their performances.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak credited Devdutt Padikkal's preparation and improved back-foot game after the left-hander produced a composed unbeaten 131 to put India in a strong position on the opening day of the first Test against Sri Lanka. Padikkal, batting at No. 3, brought up his maiden international hundred as India reached 288 for two at stumps.
Padikkal's innings was built around calculated shot selection and an ability to adapt to Sri Lanka's spin-heavy attack. Kotak said the 26-year-old had specifically worked on his back-foot game during his preparations at the BCCI Centre of Excellence, while also developing his options against turning deliveries.
“I am so happy for him because he was actually waiting for his opportunity. The way he played here and in the warm-up match, it's really encouraging,” Kotak said at the post-day press conference.
Back-foot game key to Padikkal's success
Kotak explained that Padikkal's preparation had focused on developing multiple ways of putting pressure on spinners, particularly when the pitch offered turn. The batter's ability to move back and create room, combined with occasional use of the sweep and charge down the track, allowed him to keep Sri Lanka's bowlers from settling into a rhythm.
“Preparation, I would say, overall the way Devdutt, was preparing and I saw it in the NCA (BCCI CoE)…he was working on his back foot game. We try that when we expect a turn from a pitch.
“We also tried to work on step-out, sweep besides the back foot game. So, a lot of credit goes to him, the way he has prepared himself for the last couple of years,” he added.
Padikkal's innings reflected that preparation. He was predominantly comfortable playing off the back foot but was also willing to step out when he needed to dominate the spinners.
No. 3 debate remains open
Padikkal's century could also add another dimension to India's selection decisions once regular No. 3 Sai Sudharsan returns from his toe injury. Kotak, however, suggested the team is less concerned about rigid batting positions and more focused on how players adapt to match situations.
“I think Devdutt batted really well. So Sai also has been batting really well at that number. But the thing is they all are new ball batsmen. So they open, they go number three, so, we are very flexible.
“But I would look at the way they bat, how they are adapting to conditions, how they are dealing with the different stages of a match, and that is very important for me rather than number three or four or five,” he added.
Sri Lanka also impressed by Padikkal
Padikkal's performance drew praise from Sri Lanka's spin and fielding coach Jordan Gregory, who felt the Indian batter and 
KL Rahul
 had successfully put pressure back on the hosts. Rahul also made a significant contribution before retiring hurt.
“I think firstly, credit to Padikkal. I think that he batted superbly today and so did KL. Unfortunate for him to get injured,” Gregory said.
Gregory also praised debutant off-spinner Keshara Nuwantha for the way he handled the challenge of bowling against India's batters.
“It’s very encouraging to see that Kesh on his debut had asked a lot of questions and created a lot of opportunities.
“So credit to him. I could imagine there may have been a couple of nerves from his side. But I'm very proud of him and the way he bowled on his debut,” he added.
